findings.where: First screen, the hero photograph's treatment (desktop and phone; the method set out in the Texture specimen)
findings.fault: The lectern photo has its event backdrop keyed out to flat slate, so what is left is a huge cut-out head on a plain field. Nothing of the venue, the lectern or the audience survives except the bottom of a microphone. The 'Mark at work' direction promised 'a full-bleed photograph of Mark speaking … real people in real light', but this reads as a studio headshot pasted onto a colour, like a campaign poster. The hard keyed edge around the hair and shoulders adds to the pasted look.
findings.who_objects: A senior development-bank official takes a candidate-poster look as salesy, not as a working advisor seen at a real event. The founder would object too: the brief lists slick and salesy as failures, and this is the one lever that set v7 apart.

findings.where: First screen, the lede under the heading ('I advise multilateral development banks …')
findings.fault: The only line saying what Mark does never mentions law or legal drafting. It also gives no base country and no region of his work. All it offers is generic 'advise … on infrastructure', which any infrastructure consultancy could say.
findings.who_objects: The visitor is looking for an independent legal advisor on a PPP law. After the first screen they can't tell that he is a lawyer or where he has worked, so they have no reason to write rather than keep searching. The brief says the look must reflect law, PPP and advice to governments, and the trust checklist (items 2 and 6) asks for what, for whom and where.

findings.where: Article specimen, the numbers of the three-item ordered list
findings.fault: The list numbers are house blue, which the page keeps for links. The page's own margin note says 'blue only where something can be clicked', and these numbers can't be clicked.
findings.who_objects: A reader who has learned that blue means a link either tries the numbers or starts to doubt the cue. Angélique will copy this pattern into every list she adds.

findings.where: Article specimen, the lecture row ('Streamlining the PPP Process … · PDF') at the end of the article
findings.fault: A lecture appears straight after the blog post's last line. It has no label or heading saying what it is or why it is there, so it reads as part of this article. It also sits about 4 px further in than the article's left edge.
findings.who_objects: A reader who reaches the end of the post can't tell whether this is the post's attachment, a related talk or a list of talks. This is the depth the research calls the product (a.6), and here it looks like an afterthought.

findings.fault: 'Articles and talks' and 'Blog' sit side by side as two destinations with no visible difference. There is no 'Contact' item, even though getting in touch is the page's one action.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who wants Mark's writing on PPP law has to guess which of the two items holds it. One who scrolls away from the hero finds no standing route to write to him until the footer. The first-visit trust rule asks for a 'Contact' label in the navigation.

findings.where: Header lockup, 'Mark M. Moseley' beside the reversed MMM Infra mark
findings.fault: The name is set small and light, while the white arches mark beside it is larger and heavier. So the firm's mark outweighs the person's name. The name also isn't a link, though it looks like the nav text next to it and the mark beside it does link home.
findings.who_objects: The founder, because the personal-advisor test asks that 'his name leads, with the logo beside it'. A visitor who clicks the name, as on most personal sites, gets nothing.

findings.where: Article specimen title 'The World's Best …' (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The display title uses a straight typewriter apostrophe, while the body text uses curly quotes and apostrophes. At display size the mismatch is plain.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader of legal prose sees it as a typesetting slip in the most prominent line of the article. Angélique's titles would carry the same fault.

findings.where: Page-wide left edge: the hero at about 58 px from the edge against every section below it and the footer at about 170 px (desktop)
findings.fault: The hero's content and everything below it hang from two different left edges. As the page scrolls, the content shifts inward, and the hero and the rest of the site don't line up.
findings.who_objects: Few visitors would name it, but it makes the hero look like it belongs to a different page from the article and footer below it.
